div.div: So the PTY is a compatibility layer. It exists so a program written for a 1970s serial terminal still works unchanged when the “terminal” is a window on your screen.

text.tspan: echo "ls -l" | bash // no pty required
So the PTY is a compatibility layer. It exists so a program
written for a 1970s serial terminal still works unchanged when
the “terminal” is a window on your screen.

div.span: Rescuing a broken desktop. If your GUI won’t start after a bad driver or config change (a common one is NVIDIA drivers), switch to tty3 and fix it. You can reinstall packages, edit config files, or roll back an update.

br.style: box-sizing: border-box; font-family: "Mona Sans VF", -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", "Noto Sans Backtick Fix", "Noto Sans", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, "Apple Color Emoji", "Segoe UI Emoji"; font-size: 14px; text-align: start;

div.span: Killing a frozen desktop. If the screen is hung, Ctrl+Alt+F3, log in, then kill the stuck app or restart the display manager (sudo systemctl restart gdm, sddm, or lightdm).

br.style: box-sizing: border-box; font-family: "Mona Sans VF", -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", "Noto Sans Backtick Fix", "Noto Sans", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, "Apple Color Emoji", "Segoe UI Emoji"; font-size: 14px; text-align: start;

div.span: Running without a GUI. You can install updates, run builds, or run servers with less RAM and CPU used by the desktop.

div.span: Several separate sessions. Each of tty1 to tty6 is its own login. You can run different things in each and switch with Ctrl+Alt+F1 through F6.

br.style: box-sizing: border-box; font-family: "Mona Sans VF", -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", "Noto Sans Backtick Fix", "Noto Sans", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, "Apple Color Emoji", "Segoe UI Emoji"; font-size: 14px; text-align: start;

div.span: Learning and debugging. It’s a clean environment to see how the system behaves with no desktop in the way.

text.tspan: When it’s actually useful
Rescuing a broken desktop. If your GUI won’t start after a bad driver or config change (a common
one is NVIDIA drivers), switch to tty3 and fix it. You can reinstall packages, edit config files, or roll
back an update.
Killing a frozen desktop. If the screen is hung, Ctrl+Alt+F3, log in, then kill the stuck app or restart
the display manager (sudo systemctl restart gdm, sddm, or lightdm).
Running without a GUI. You can install updates, run builds, or run servers with less RAM and
CPU used by the desktop.
Several separate sessions. Each of tty1 to tty6 is its own login. You can run different things in
each and switch with Ctrl+Alt+F1 through F6.
Learning and debugging. It’s a clean environment to see how the system behaves with no
desktop in the way.

div.p:
1. Pretends to be a terminal device. The program sees /dev/pts/N and isatty() returns true.
2. Carries data both ways. Your keystrokes go in, and the program’s output comes back out.
3. Runs the kernel’s terminal logic in between. This is called the line discipline. It handles echo, backspace, Ctrl+C turning into a SIGINT signal, and raw vs. line mode. It also holds the window size (rows and columns).

text.tspan: PTY does three jobs:
1. Pretends to be a terminal device. The program sees /dev/pts/N and isatty()
returns true.
2. Carries data both ways. Your keystrokes go in, and the program’s output comes
back out.
3. Runs the kernel’s terminal logic in between. This is called the line discipline. It
handles echo, backspace, Ctrl+C turning into a SIGINT signal, and raw vs. line
mode. It also holds the window size (rows and columns).

h2.span: why not to use tty directly

p.style: box-sizing: border-box; margin-top: 0px; margin-bottom: 16px; font-family: "Mona Sans VF", -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", "Noto Sans Backtick Fix", "Noto Sans", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, "Apple Color Emoji", "Segoe UI Emoji"; font-size: 14px; text-align: start;

span.style: background-color: light-dark(rgb(33, 40, 48), rgb(0, 0, 0));

p.span: Because a real TTY’s other end is fixed hardware, and you can’t put your own program there.

ol.style: box-sizing: border-box; margin-top: 0px; padding: 0px; position: relative; font-family: "Mona Sans VF", -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", "Noto Sans Backtick Fix", "Noto Sans", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, "Apple Color Emoji", "Segoe UI Emoji"; font-size: 14px; text-align: start; background-color: light-dark(rgb(33, 40, 48), rgb(199, 205, 212)); margin-bottom: 0px !important;

span.style: background-color: light-dark(rgb(33, 40, 48), rgb(0, 0, 0));

p.span:
Limited number, tied to the physical machine.
Linux has only a handful of virtual consoles (tty1 to tty6), all sharing one keyboard and one screen, and only one is visible at a time. You couldn’t have 20 terminal tabs, 50 SSH users, or a terminal per browser session.

span.style: background-color: light-dark(rgb(33, 40, 48), rgb(0, 0, 0));

p.span:
The output goes to hardware, not to your program.
If you write to /dev/tty3, the kernel sends the text to the screen. Your terminal app (iTerm, VS Code, a browser terminal) never sees it, so it can’t draw it in its own window. Likewise, keystrokes come from the physical keyboard, not from your app. There’s no place for a program to sit in the middle and say “I’ll provide the input and read the output.”

span.style: background-color: light-dark(rgb(33, 40, 48), rgb(0, 0, 0));

p.span:
No remote access.
When you SSH in, your keyboard is on another computer. The server’s kernel has no hardware path to it. sshd needs a terminal that it can feed with your keystrokes (received over the network) and read output from (to send back over the network). Only a PTY lets a program do that.

span.style: background-color: light-dark(rgb(33, 40, 48), rgb(0, 0, 0));

p.span:
Programs expect a TTY.
bash, vim and ssh need the terminal features we covered: raw mode, signals, window size. So you can’t just give them a plain pipe. You need something that is a TTY but is controlled by software.

text.tspan: why not to use tty directly
Because a real TTY’s other end is fixed hardware, and you can’t put your own program there.
Limited number, tied to the physical machine.

Linux has only a handful of virtual consoles (tty1 to tty6), all sharing one keyboard and one screen, and only one is visible at a time. You couldn’t have 20 terminal tabs, 50 SSH users, or a terminal
per browser session.The output goes to hardware, not to your program.

If you write to /dev/tty3, the kernel sends the text to the screen. Your terminal app (iTerm, VS Code, a browser terminal) never sees it, so it can’t draw it in its own window. Likewise, keystrokes come
from the physical keyboard, not from your app. There’s no place for a program to sit in the middle and say “I’ll provide the input and read the output.”No remote access.
When you SSH in, your keyboard is on another computer. The server’s kernel has no hardware path to it. sshd needs a terminal that it can feed with your keystrokes (received over the network) and
read output from (to send back over the network). Only a PTY lets a program do that.Programs expect a TTY.
bash, vim and ssh need the terminal features we covered: raw mode, signals, window size. So you can’t just give them a plain pipe. You need something that is a TTY but is controlled by software.
